items.prompt: Before the patch, parsePositiveInt used Number.parseInt. What did ?price_min=12px become, and why is that wrong for this contract?
items.answer: priceMin 12, because parseInt reads the numeric prefix and ignores the rest
distractors: undefined, because parseInt returns NaN for any string that contains letters
priceMin 0, because parseInt treats unparseable input as zero
A thrown RangeError that the route turned into a 400 response
items.explanation: A prefix parser answers 'what number starts this string?'; this contract asks 'is the whole string a non-negative integer that Number represents exactly?' - so 12px, 12.9 and ' 12' all used to become 12.

items.prompt: The new parser checks value.length === 0 before the /\D/ test. What would ?price_min= (empty) produce without that guard?
distractors: undefined
A crash in the regex test
priceMin 1
items.explanation: /\D/.test("") is false (an empty string contains no non-digit) and Number("") is 0, so without the length guard an empty bound becomes a real priceMin of 0; removing it makes test 2 fail.

items.prompt: Why does the parser use Number.isSafeInteger rather than Number.isFinite for ?price_min=9007199254740992?
items.answer: It is finite but not exactly representable, and isSafeInteger rejects it
distractors: isFinite would reject it as Infinity, so either check works here
isSafeInteger also rejects 0, which the contract wants to exclude
Number.isFinite does not exist as a static method on Number in Node 22
items.explanation: 2^53 is beyond MAX_SAFE_INTEGER; swapping in Number.isFinite makes test 2 fail.

items.prompt: In JavaScript, what does /^\d+$/.test("12\n") return, and what does that mean for swapping /\D/ for !/^\d+$/?
items.answer: false: without the m flag, $ matches only at the end of input, so both forms work
distractors: true: $ matches before a final line terminator, so the anchored form is unsafe
true, but only on Windows, where the input arrives ending in CRLF
It throws, because \d is not valid inside an anchored pattern without the u flag
items.explanation: The guide corrects its own earlier claim: the 'dollar before final newline' edge exists in Python, Perl and PCRE, not JS. The LF/CRLF tests stay to guard against someone adding the m flag.

items.prompt: The URL contains price_min=12px&price_min=5. What priceMin does the parser produce?
items.answer: None: only the first value is read, and 12px is rejected
distractors: 5, because the parser skips invalid values and takes the next valid one
12, because the first value's numeric prefix is still used
5, because the last value of a repeated query parameter wins
items.explanation: Exercise 6 observed priceMin absent: parsePositiveInt(readFirst(...)) - a malformed first value drops the bound entirely.

items.prompt: A shopper visits ?price_min=500&price_max=10. What reaches Spree?
distractors: The bounds swapped: 10 to 500
Neither bound
The route rejects the request with a 400 validation error
items.explanation: Finding F2: nothing between the URL and Spree checks ordering, so the listing is guaranteed empty and looks like 'no products'. A fix states its chosen behavior (drop both, swap, or drop one) with a dedicated test.

items.prompt: A crawler requests ?sort=anything-goes. What happens, and why does it matter even though the UI only offers Spree's sort options?
items.answer: It is forwarded to Spree, and each junk value is its own listingKey and cache entry
distractors: It is dropped, because sortBy is checked against an allowlist just like availability
It is replaced with manual, the storefront's default sort order
The request fails with a 400 from Spree before anything is cached
items.explanation: Finding F1: availability has an allowlist (isAvailabilityStatus) but sortBy is any non-empty trimmed string; only "manual" is filtered out before Spree.

items.prompt: Spree delivers the same order.completed event twice, concurrently, to one instance. How many confirmation emails can go out?
items.answer: Two: both pass the check before either reaches markProcessed
distractors: One: the in-memory Set makes processing exactly-once per event id
One: Node is single-threaded, so the second delivery waits for the first to finish
Zero: concurrent duplicate deliveries are rejected by the signature check
items.explanation: Finding F3: check at line 47, await sendEmail, mark at line 90 - a check-then-act window. Mark-after-send is deliberate (failed sends retry) but gives at-least-once, and a restart or second instance forgets the Set entirely.

items.prompt: Two URLs differ only in the order of option=red&option=large. Are they the same listing state, and the same URL?
items.answer: Same state, because listingKey sorts optionValues, but different URLs
distractors: Different state and different URLs, because option order changes Spree's results
Same URL and same state, because URLSearchParams sorts repeated keys
Same URL but different state, because listingKey keeps insertion order
items.explanation: Finding F4: harmless today, but worth knowing before anyone uses the raw URL as a cache key.

items.prompt: cachedListProducts takes a _userToken argument that it never passes to the SDK. Why is it there?
items.answer: It becomes part of the cache key, separating guests from users
distractors: It is dead code left over from an earlier version of the SDK
The SDK reads it implicitly from the closure scope of the function
It authorizes the request against Spree's product list endpoint
items.explanation: Arguments form the cache key of a "use cache" function; passing the token (guests pass undefined) segments cached product lists so authenticated users do not share entries with guests.

items.prompt: Why does CartContext skip refreshCart on the /order-placed/ page?
items.answer: getCart would clear the guest's cart token cookie before the order page can use it
distractors: Refreshing would re-add the purchased items to a brand-new cart for the shopper
The order-placed page is statically rendered and cannot call server actions
To save one network request on a page that does not show the cart drawer
items.explanation: Navigation behavior and token lifetime are coupled - getCompletedOrder likewise avoids getCart() for the same reason.

items.prompt: The webhook handler reads the body with request.text(), verifies the signature, and only then calls JSON.parse. Why that order?
items.answer: The signature covers the raw bytes, and unverified input should not be parsed
distractors: JSON.parse is slow, so verifying first is purely a performance optimization
request.json() is unavailable inside Next.js route handlers
The event name needed for verification lives inside the JSON body
items.explanation: Missing headers answer 401, an invalid signature answers 401, and only then is the verified text parsed (invalid JSON answers 400).

items.front: The listing parser silently drops a malformed price bound instead of returning an error. Why is that defensible, and what would change it?
items.back: It follows the module's existing convention - an unknown availability value is treated as absent (listing-search-params.ts:73-77). Silent omission is a policy; a visible validation error would be a NEW contract with tests at the route boundary.

items.front: Name three things the URL filter parser cannot promise, and where each belongs.
items.back: It cannot authorize a customer (route), prove a price range is sensible (query builder), or make the ten-minute-cached catalog response fresh (cache/Spree) - it only drops malformed filters.

items.front: Where does cart state live in this storefront, and which function centralizes every mutation?
items.back: Spree owns the durable cart record (server actions in lib/data/cart.ts), HTTP-only cookies hold cart id and token, and React Context mirrors the session view. mutateCart sets updating, runs the server action, mirrors result.cart into state, then router.refresh() - or toasts the error.
